title: Middleware and the Request Pipeline
summary: Learn what middleware is, why its order matters, and how to write your own for request ids, timing, and errors.
intro: Every request Roombook answers needs the same chores done around it. It needs an id, so you can find it in the logs. It needs a log line saying how long it took, security headers, a CORS check for the web app, its JSON body read, and a clean answer when something crashes. Writing those into every handler would copy the same lines dozens of times, and the one handler that forgets them becomes the hole. **Middleware** is how a server does each chore once, for every request. This lesson explains what middleware is and why its order matters. Then you write your own for request ids and timing, add one place that turns every crash into a clean answer, and meet the middleware Express and its packages give you.

steps.title: What middleware is

examples.title: A middleware that never calls next
examples.prompt: With the forgetful middleware first in `src/app.ts`, ask for the rooms. The `-m 3` gives up after three seconds, and `-sS` hides curl's progress but keeps its errors.
examples.output: curl: (28) Operation timed out after 3005 milliseconds with 0 bytes received
examples.explanation: curl waited three seconds for a single byte and got nothing. The server's terminal shows `GET /v1/rooms`, so the middleware ran, but it neither answered nor called `next()`, and Express has no way to know you meant to. The request just sits there, holding its connection open, until the client gives up. A browser would show a spinner for minutes. This is the first thing to check when a request hangs in an Express app: a middleware on its path that has a branch where it neither responds nor calls `next()`. A `return` before `next()` in an `if` is the usual culprit.

steps.title: Order matters

examples.title: Body parsing registered too late
examples.prompt: In this version of the app, the `POST /v1/bookings` route comes before `app.use(express.json())`, and the handler reads `req.body.roomId`. Send it a booking.
examples.explanation: The request reached the handler before `express.json()` had run, so `req.body` was still `undefined`, and reading `.roomId` from it threw `TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'roomId')`. Express 5 passed that error to the error handler from part 4, which logged it and answered this 500. Nothing about the route itself is wrong, which is what makes the bug confusing: the same handler works the moment the line moves up. When a handler finds `req.body` empty or `undefined`, check that a body parser runs before it, and that the request's `Content-Type` is one that parser reads.

steps.title: Your own middleware: request ids and timing

examples.title: An id made, and an id kept
examples.prompt: Ask for the rooms twice: once with no id, and once sending your own. `grep` keeps only the id header from each response.
examples.code: curl -si localhost:4000/v1/rooms | grep -i "^x-request-id"; curl -si -H "X-Request-Id: demo-42" localhost:4000/v1/rooms | grep -i "^x-request-id"
examples.explanation: The first request had no `X-Request-Id`, so the middleware made a UUID and sent it back. The second sent `demo-42`, which passes the check, so the server kept it, and both log lines above use these same ids. A proxy that already gives each request an id keeps it all the way through, and a client that sends its own can quote it to support without reading any header. Try sending an id with a space or a semicolon in it, and you get a fresh UUID instead.

examples.title: A write in read-only mode
examples.prompt: Start the server with `READ_ONLY=true` in the environment, and try to create a booking. The `grep -v` hides the security headers from part 5.
examples.output:
HTTP/1.1 503 Service Unavailable
X-Request-Id: e49167f4-54fb-4c31-bd02-4a3abf08dd10
Retry-After: 600
Content-Type: application/json; charset=utf-8
Content-Length: 62
Date: Sat, 21 Nov 2026 23:45:00 GMT

{"status":503,"title":"Roombook is read-only for maintenance"}
examples.explanation: The middleware answered by itself: `503 Service Unavailable` with `Retry-After: 600`, ten minutes, and the booking route never ran. A well-behaved client waits that long and tries again, instead of hammering a server that's busy. The request still has an `X-Request-Id`, because the request id layer sits outside the read-only one, so even this refusal can be found in the logs. A `GET` goes through as usual, since reading changes nothing. The error body is a first draft: the next lesson replaces it with the standard error format every Roombook error uses.

steps.title: Catching errors in one place

examples.title: A path that doesn't exist, and a crash
examples.prompt: Ask for a path no route has, then for a test route whose handler throws `new Error("database is down")`.
examples.explanation: The first answer came from `notFound`, in JSON like every other answer from the API. The second came from `errorHandler`: a generic 500 with the request id, and not a word about the database. The server's terminal has the rest, a JSON line with the same request id, `"level":"error"`, and the full stack trace, pointing at the line in `src/app.ts` that threw. That split is the point. The person who can fix the bug gets every detail, under an id the user can quote, and the person on the other end of the request gets nothing they could use against you.

steps.title: Middleware from Express and its packages
steps.body:
Most of the middleware an Express API runs, you don't write. Express ships a few, and the rest come from npm packages that nearly every Express API installs. Knowing what exists saves you from writing a worse copy of it.

## Built into Express

- `express.json()`, `express.urlencoded()`, `express.text()`, and `express.raw()` parse bodies of each kind, each with a `limit`. The reliability lesson uses `express.raw()`, since checking a webhook's signature needs the body's exact bytes.
- `express.static("public")` serves files from a folder. A JSON API rarely needs it.
- `express.Router()` makes a mini app with its own middleware and routes, which you mount with `app.use(path, router)`.

## Packages nearly every API adds

| Package | What it does | In this course |
|---|---|---|
| `helmet` | Sets a dozen security headers in one line | Now, and the security lesson |
| `cors` | Answers preflights and sets the CORS headers from an allowlist | Now |
| `compression` | Compresses large responses with gzip | Often done by a proxy instead |
| `pino-http` | Fast JSON request logging, with a request id | Replaces the hand-written logger in the lesson on deploying |
| `express-rate-limit` | Limits requests per client | The Redis lesson |
| `multer` | Reads file uploads, sent as `multipart/form-data` | When you need uploads |
| `express-session` | Server-side sessions in a cookie | The authentication lesson |

Express has no timeout middleware built in. Node's HTTP server gives every request five minutes by default, through `server.requestTimeout`, which the reliability lesson tightens along with the timeouts on calls the API makes.

## Middleware factories

Notice that almost all of these are *called* when you register them: `helmet()`, `cors({ origin })`, `express.json({ limit: "100kb" })`. Each is a **factory**, a function that takes options and returns the middleware. The options are read once, at startup, and the middleware they produce runs on every request. `readOnlyMode(config.readOnly)` from part 3 follows the same pattern, and it's the one to copy for your own: settings come in as arguments, so `createApp` decides them, and a test can build the app with read-only mode on, without touching the environment.

## Middleware and the event loop

Every middleware runs on Node's single JavaScript thread, on every request, so the rule from Your First Express Project matters most here. Something slow in one, like reading a file with `fs.readFileSync` or hashing a password with a synchronous function, blocks every other request on the server while it runs. Keep middleware quick, and anything slow `async`.

The next lesson checks every input against a schema, and grows the error handler from part 4 into one that answers every error in one standard format.

examples.title: The headers helmet adds
examples.prompt: Ask for the rooms with `-I`, which shows only the status line and the headers.
examples.output:
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
X-Request-Id: 42c4ae34-8969-4bd1-a7ed-45701e845c66
Content-Security-Policy: default-src 'self';base-uri 'self';font-src 'self' https: data:;form-action 'self';frame-ancestors 'self';img-src 'self' data:;object-src 'none';script-src 'self';script-src-attr 'none';style-src 'self' https: 'unsafe-inline';upgrade-insecure-requests
Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy: same-origin
Cross-Origin-Resource-Policy: same-origin
Origin-Agent-Cluster: ?1
Referrer-Policy: no-referrer
Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=31536000; includeSubDomains
X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff
X-DNS-Prefetch-Control: off
X-Download-Options: noopen
X-Frame-Options: SAMEORIGIN
X-Permitted-Cross-Domain-Policies: none
X-XSS-Protection: 0
Access-Control-Allow-Origin: http://localhost:5173
Vary: Origin
Content-Type: application/json; charset=utf-8
Content-Length: 67
ETag: W/"43-rhCNVUwMAW3DF6NcEMeonR6kFqE"
Date: Sat, 21 Nov 2026 23:44:55 GMT
Connection: keep-alive
Keep-Alive: timeout=5
examples.explanation: Everything from `Content-Security-Policy` to `X-XSS-Protection` came from one line, `app.use(helmet())`. Most of them tell a browser how to treat what it receives. `Strict-Transport-Security` is the HSTS header from the web course: only use `https` for this site, for a year. `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff` says trust the `Content-Type` and never guess. `X-Frame-Options` stops other sites from showing your pages inside theirs. For a JSON API, `Content-Security-Policy` matters less than for a site, but it costs nothing. Notice what isn't there: `X-Powered-By: Express`, which Express sends by default. The `app.disable` line turns it off, and helmet removes it too, so the response doesn't announce which framework to look up weaknesses for. `ETag` is Express's own, from the request data lesson.

examples.title: A CORS preflight
examples.prompt: Act like the browser running Roombook's web app on `localhost:5173`: send the OPTIONS preflight it sends before a POST with a JSON body. `grep` keeps the status line and the CORS headers.
examples.code: curl -si -X OPTIONS localhost:4000/v1/bookings -H "Origin: http://localhost:5173" -H "Access-Control-Request-Method: POST" -H "Access-Control-Request-Headers: content-type" | grep -iE "^(HTTP|access-control|vary)"
examples.output:
HTTP/1.1 204 No Content
Access-Control-Allow-Origin: http://localhost:5173
Vary: Origin, Access-Control-Request-Headers
Access-Control-Allow-Methods: GET,HEAD,PUT,PATCH,POST,DELETE
Access-Control-Allow-Headers: content-type
examples.explanation: The `cors()` middleware answered the preflight itself, with `204 No Content`, and the request never reached a route. `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` names the one origin `createApp` allowed, so the browser lets the web app's real POST go ahead. `Access-Control-Allow-Methods` lists what the package allows by default, and `Access-Control-Allow-Headers` echoes the `content-type` the browser asked about. `Vary` tells caches the answer depends on those request headers, so a cached answer for one site is never handed to another. A preflight from any other origin gets no `Access-Control-Allow-Origin`, and the browser blocks the call.

recap:
- Middleware is code that runs around every handler, for jobs that cut across all routes, like ids, logs, headers, and errors.
- The pipeline is an onion: each layer works on the way in, calls the rest, and works again on the way out.
- A middleware can read the request, add to it, answer early, or act on the response, and forgetting to pass the request on is a classic bug.
- Order is design: request id and logging outermost, CORS before anything that refuses, body parsing before handlers, errors at the edge.
- A request id, kept from X-Request-Id when it's safe or made fresh, ties a request's log lines together and goes back to the client.
- Per-request values live in res.locals, never in globals, since one server works on many requests at once.
- One error handler logs the details and answers a generic 500 with the request id, and unknown paths get a JSON 404.
- Scope middleware to where it's needed: the whole app, a group of routes, or one route.
